The Apostolic Canons: primacy and mutual consent

Foundations · The Church and Tradition

The Apostolic Canons: primacy and mutual consent

5 sectionsNot completed
Notes

This selection from the collection called the Apostolic Canons describes ordination, territorial responsibility and cooperation among bishops. Synodality means the exercise of church responsibilities through common deliberation; the collection’s title is retained without assigning a new date or authorship to it.[1]

Who ordains a bishop?[1]

Canon I specifies two or three bishops for the ordination of a bishop. The rule distinguishes episcopal ordination from the ordination of other clergy in the next canon.[1]

Read original passage

Apostolic Canons: Canon I

Complete named canons of the late-antique collection traditionally titled the Apostolic Canons, in Percival’s 1900 volume. The traditional title is not a claim that the surviving collection was personally written by the Twelve. Historical numbering variants are retained.

Canon I.

Let a bishop be ordained by two or three bishops.

Who ordains priests and deacons?[1]

Canon II assigns the ordination of a presbyter, deacon and other clergy to one bishop. Presbyter is the term commonly translated priest in this context.[1]

Read original passage

Apostolic Canons: Canon II

Complete named canons of the late-antique collection traditionally titled the Apostolic Canons, in Percival’s 1900 volume. The traditional title is not a claim that the surviving collection was personally written by the Twelve. Historical numbering variants are retained.

Canon II.

Let a presbyter, deacon, and the rest of the clergy, be ordained by one bishop,

How is a leading bishop related to the other bishops?[1]

Canon XXXIV requires the bishops to recognize the one who is first among them and to obtain his consent for matters of consequence. It equally requires that leading bishop to act with the others’ consent. The rule describes reciprocal responsibilities, while reserving a bishop’s ordinary local affairs to his own care.[1]

Read original passage

Apostolic Canons: Canon XXXIV

Complete named canons of the late-antique collection traditionally titled the Apostolic Canons, in Percival’s 1900 volume. The traditional title is not a claim that the surviving collection was personally written by the Twelve. Historical numbering variants are retained.

Canon XXXIV. (XXXV.)

The bishops of every nation must acknowledge him who is first among them and account him as their head, and do nothing of consequence without his consent; but each may do those things only which concern his own parish, and the country places which belong to it. But neither let him (who is the first) do anything without the consent of all; for so there will be unanimity, and God will be glorified through the Lord in the Holy Spirit.

Why do territorial boundaries matter?[1]

Canon XXXV restricts ordination in places outside a bishop’s authority without the consent of those responsible there. It therefore connects ordination with a defined responsibility for a particular church territory.[1]

Read original passage

Apostolic Canons: Canon XXXV

Complete named canons of the late-antique collection traditionally titled the Apostolic Canons, in Percival’s 1900 volume. The traditional title is not a claim that the surviving collection was personally written by the Twelve. Historical numbering variants are retained.

Canon XXXV. (XXXVI.)

Let not a bishop dare to ordain beyond his own limits, in cities and places not subject to him. But if he be convicted of doing so, without the consent of those persons who have authority over such cities and places, let him be deposed, and those also whom he has ordained.

What is the work of regular episcopal meetings?[1]

Canon XXXVII describes meetings of bishops for examining religious decrees and resolving church controversies. Its twice-yearly schedule is part of the historical text. The essential subject is the common consideration of questions that arise among the churches.[1]

Read original passage

Apostolic Canons: Canon XXXVII

Complete named canons of the late-antique collection traditionally titled the Apostolic Canons, in Percival’s 1900 volume. The traditional title is not a claim that the surviving collection was personally written by the Twelve. Historical numbering variants are retained.

Canon XXXVII. (XXXVIII.)

Let there be a meeting of the bishops twice a year, and let them examine amongst themselves the decrees concerning religion and settle the ecclesiastical controversies which may have occurred. One meeting to be held in the fourth week of Pentecost [i.e., the fourth week after Easter], and the other on the 12th day of the month Hyperberetæus [i.e., October].

Scripture

1 Peter 5:1–4

The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed:

Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;

Neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.

And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
